title: Extending an Experiment
subtitle: From twenty planets that the engine ran to a population of two hundred thousand, with every uncertainty, in Python on the compute page
body:
Step 1 of 8 read

Twenty planets that the engine ran

The Binary Planet Lab puts a planet near one star of a pair that is ten astronomical units apart. An experiment on the experiment runner ran twenty trials of it: in each the planet started at a distance from its star drawn at random between 0.12 and 0.42 of the stars' separation, and the engine ran it for about twenty orbits of the binary. Some planets stayed in orbit and some were thrown out.

The experiment's result is a file, and the notebook reads it. It calls a planet bound if its mean distance from the star stayed within a cutoff (three, to start) times the distance it started at, fits the chance of being bound as a smooth curve of the starting distance, repeats the fit on 400 resamples of the twenty to get its uncertainty, and draws two hundred thousand synthetic planets to say how many would stay bound in a larger population.

Open the compute page at /compute/ of this site. It is online only and downloads about 19 MB of Python the first time, when you press the button. Choose the notebook A population of planets, extended, keep its example input (the twenty planets), and its settings at slope 1, 200,000 planets and cutoff 3. Do not press Run yet.

title: Extending an Experiment
subtitle: From twenty planets that the engine ran to a population of two hundred thousand, with every uncertainty, in Python on the compute page
body:
Step 8 of 8 read

What you worked out

Twenty planets, run by the engine, fixed the edge of the bound region to about 0.255 ± 0.024 of the stars' separation. Extended to two hundred thousand synthetic planets, the bound fraction was 0.596 ± 0.076 for a population with equal numbers per factor of distance, and 0.451 ± 0.081 for a uniform one, which is where the sample's own 0.6 should have been.

What the numbers do not say: the interval counts the scatter of twenty trials and nothing else. It does not count the choice of a logistic curve, the definition of bound, or the draw's range, outside of which no synthetic planet is made. A larger synthetic population has a smaller sampling error and exactly the same assumptions. The run is yours to keep: its capsule records the notebook's hash and the result file's, so a report can cite it.
